solution:
Settled by the chapter's own worked rule and example.

The text states: "While travelling from Japan to America, we need to consider the existing day and date even after crossing the IDL... On the contrary, while going from America to Japan, and crossing the IDL, one needs to add a day to the date. So if it is Thursday, 25th December then it will be Friday, 26th December."

The chapter fixes the geography explicitly: Japan lies to the WEST of the IDL and America lies to the EAST of it ("Shyamrao left for America (which lies to the east of the IDL) from Japan (from the west of the IDL)"). So the journey that ADDS a day — America to Japan — is a journey from EAST to WEST.

The pair of worked examples confirms the asymmetry. Going west-to-east (Japan to America), Shyamrao left on Monday 1st at 1 p.m., flew 24 hours, and still arrived on "Monday 1st, 1 pm" — a full day was subtracted. Going east-to-west (America to Japan), he left Friday 5th at 12 noon and arrived "Saturday 6th 12 noon" — the day advanced.

Hence a day is added when travelling East to West. Answer: A.

Computed from the chapter's own time-and-longitude rule.

The chapter establishes: "The earth takes 24 hours to make one rotation (Earth takes 24 hours to make a round of 360 degrees around itself). Earth rotates from west to east. Therefore, in terms of time the eastern part of the earth is ahead of the western part."

So 360 degrees corresponds to 24 hours = 1440 minutes, giving 1440 / 360 = 4 minutes of time per degree of longitude.

Arithmetic:
- Given meridian: 15 degrees E. Target: the IDL, drawn with reference to the 180 degree meridian.
- Longitude difference = 180 - 15 = 165 degrees (both measured eastward from Greenwich, so we simply subtract).
- Time difference = 165 x 4 minutes = 660 minutes = 660 / 60 = 11 hours.
- Direction: the IDL (180 degrees) lies EAST of 15 degrees E, and eastern places are AHEAD in time, so the 11 hours must be ADDED.
- Time at the IDL = Wednesday 10:00 a.m. + 11 hours = Wednesday 21:00 hrs = Wednesday 9 p.m.

The date does not roll over, because 10 a.m. + 11 h = 9 p.m. on the same day. Answer: B (Wednesday 9 p.m.).

Cross-check against the chapter's own worked figures: Sunil starts at 0 degrees at 12 noon Thursday and the text says "at 90 degrees E meridian, it will be Thursday 6 pm" — 90 x 4 min = 360 min = 6 hours added to 12 noon, giving 6 p.m. The same rule applied here gives 11 hours.

Directly settled by the text.

Describing the 1884 decision taken by representatives of many nations under the leadership of American professor Davidson, the chapter says: "The line was drawn opposite to the Greenwich Prime Meridian i.e. with reference to the 180 degree meridian. It is an international convention to change the day and time while crossing this line."

Earlier the same point is made: "According to the convention, the start (and end) of a date is considered to be at 180 degree meridian," and "maximum part of the IDL coincides with the 180 degree meridian."

So the internationally agreed meridian of day and date change is 180 degrees. Answer: D.

Directly settled by the text.

"We can consider that with reference to the IDL, the day on the Earth starts in the West and ends in the East. It is one and the same day only at 12 o'clock midnight at the 180 degree meridian. For the countries lying to the east of it i.e. the USA, Chile, etc., it is the end of the day while for the countries lying to the west of it i.e. Japan, Australia, etc. it is the start of a new day."

So a new day begins immediately on the WEST side of the IDL. Answer: B.

This is corroborated by the New Year table on the chapter's opening page, where the western-of-IDL locations (Samoa's Apia, Auckland, Funafuti, Sydney, Tokyo) all welcome the New Year on Saturday, while the eastern-of-IDL locations (New York, Baker Island) do so on Sunday by Indian time; and by the Q3 exercise prompt "The day starts in Pacific Ocean on the earth."

Directly settled by the section titled "The importance of IDL".

"The IDL brings coordination between international airlines, transportation services, economic and trade activities... We can keep a track of all the calculations of day and time accurately with the help of IDL in case of global transportation esp. with respect to airways. It is only because of the IDL that the schedules of the traffic worldwide are organised properly."

Of the four options, only "Transportation schedules" is named in the chapter. GPS and defence departments are never mentioned anywhere in the chapter, and determining the hemisphere is a function of the Equator and the Prime Meridian, not of the IDL. Answer: C.
